```mermaid
    TargetFlux --> Graph["CAPI + CAPMOX\ncomplete 3-node graph"]
    Graph --> PVE["Proxmox VMs\nSER9 / SER10 / AOOStar"]
    TargetFlux --> Platform["Talos CCM + platform\nGarage + CNPG + Forgejo"]
    TargetFlux --> Providers["CAPI Operator\ntarget provider set"]
    Seed["Stopped static seed\nVMs 120-122"] -. recovery reference only .-> PVE
```

### `gitops-flux-capi`
Status: current
Decision: Flux owns continuous reconciliation for the seed-to-target build and the target platform. The CAPI Helm add-on provider installs bootstrap Cilium once; target-local Flux adopts that Helm release for steady state. A dedicated Flux source/Kustomization for the CAPI lifecycle carries the clusterctl move label, so it moves with the CAPI graph and begins reconciling locally after the pivot. CAPI Operator installs the target's provider set, including the Helm add-on provider, and Flux records the matching clusterctl provider inventory before that move.
Why: Flux can consume a CAPI-generated kubeconfig directly for remote Kustomizations, so the target controllers and root can be declared alongside the Cluster without a separate cluster-registration adapter. Its controller-only model also fits the required source/Kustomize/Helm surface without adding a UI or application abstraction. The install-once CAPI add-on closes the target-CNI bootstrap cycle without creating two continuous Helm owners. Argo CD remains a valid alternative if its UI, ApplicationSet, projects, or multi-tenant policy become a real requirement.
Revisit when: Flux cannot express a required ownership relationship, or an Argo-specific operating capability becomes more valuable than the direct CAPI integration.

## Node lifecycle: CAPMOX

[Cluster API Provider Proxmox (CAPMOX)](https://github.com/ionos-cloud/cluster-api-provider-proxmox)
owns Kubernetes node VM lifecycle on Proxmox in steady state. Accepted node intent flows:

```text
Git -> Flux -> CAPI (Cluster / Machine) -> CAPMOX (ProxmoxMachine) -> Proxmox VMs
```

CAPMOX needs a Kubernetes management cluster before it can create a Kubernetes cluster. The
completed bootstrap was therefore a **parallel build and pivot**, not retroactive adoption:

```text
static seed cluster (management only)
  -> Flux applies the complete CAPI/CAPMOX target declaration
  -> CAPI Helm add-on installs target Cilium once; seed Flux installs target Flux
  -> target Flux installs the platform and the target CAPI provider set
  -> suspend the lifecycle reconciler; clusterctl moves it and the CAPI graph into the target
  -> resume that reconciler on the target
  -> static seed retires
```

The three manually built seed guests are not CAPI `Machine` objects. Installing provider
controllers or writing `Node.spec.providerID` does not make them managed. Never attach a
`TalosControlPlane` to their existing etcd ring: CACPPT v0.5.13 audits etcd membership against the
control-plane Machines it owns and can remove seed members that have no corresponding Machine.

CAPMOX owns create/replace/scale only for the separate target it creates. The target declaration
sets the intended three replicas at once; CAPI and its providers handle their own causal ordering.
The target could run applications before the management pivot. The completed `clusterctl move`
transferred the existing CAPI object graph and its movable lifecycle reconciler into the target;
it did not discover unmanaged Nodes or manufacture Machines for the seed. Target Flux now owns
both platform and lifecycle steady state.

The seed-side remote Kustomizations and Gateway API writer were the finite bootstrap path. They
were suspended and retired after target-local `homelab-target`, `target-flux-components`, and
`target-platform` adopted those resources, so only target Flux applies current desired state.

CAPMOX v0.9.0 has two material limits carried explicitly by the target design. Its clone state
machine can skip IPAM when a cloned VM needs no configuration change, so the target template adds
managed tags that force the missing transition. Proxmox cannot clone template 9000 directly from
SER10's non-shared `local-zfs` onto another host, and CAPMOX cannot map that storage to AOOStar's
`local-lvm`. The template therefore stages all three Machines on SER10; one native PVE migration to
SER9 and one to AOOStar establish the final spread. The focused contract is in
[`infra/k8s/capmox/README.md`](../../infra/k8s/capmox/README.md).

The completed pivot exposed one additional v0.9 recovery edge: recreated ProxmoxMachine resources
rediscovered already-running VMs as `Provisioned` without rebuilding their controller-owned address
status. The 2026-07-22 live repair restored only each `InternalIP` from its existing IPAddress
object. CAPMOX normally also publishes its ProxmoxMachine name as `MachineHostName`, but CACPPT uses
that address in preference to the CAPI Machine/Node identity when auditing etcd. Restoring that
hostname caused CACPPT to remove valid etcd members whose Talos hostnames correctly match their CAPI
Machines. The controller was paused, the hostname addresses were removed, and the affected members
were rejoined one at a time with an EPHEMERAL-only Talos reset. New Machines still follow the
complete IPAM path; no second address authority or standing repair controller is introduced.

### `identity-lock`
Status: current
Decision: The static seed retains pinned host-specific identities. Target nodes use their CAPI Machine name as the Talos and Kubernetes node name, while CAPMOX allocates replaceable VM identities within VMIDs 100-109.
Why: Seed identities remain understandable during the transition, while generated target identity matches controller-owned replacement semantics instead of pretending a replaceable Machine is a permanent host guest.
Revisit when: A workload requires stable node identity beyond labels and placement policy, or CAPMOX adds a stronger failure-domain identity contract.

### `capmox-accepted`
Status: current
Decision: A temporary static seed declared a separate three-member CAPMOX-native Talos target; target-local Flux established the application platform and provider set, then received the existing CAPI graph through a standard pivot. The target is now self-managing and the seed is stopped.
Why: CAPMOX is the accepted Kubernetes-native Proxmox lifecycle provider, while parallel construction avoids unsupported seed adoption and CACPPT etcd reconciliation against unmanaged members. Declaring the whole target removes the failed human-operated one-node-at-a-time build path.
Revisit when: CAPMOX cannot meet a measured lifecycle need, or a different provider is deliberately accepted.

## Stable platform vs convertible burst capacity

This domain owns the **stable** application platform: the CAPMOX-native Talos target,
platform services, and Forgejo/CNPG. Its three control planes remain distributed across the stable
SER9 / SER10 / AOOStar placement subset and are never convertible workers. The stopped static seed
is retained only as a finite rebuild reference; it is not the durable application target.

**Convertible / dual-role capacity** (N5 and later EVO as Talos worker by default, exclusive
inference LXC on demand, host-mode controller, capacity classes, min stable allocatable) is
authoritative in [N5 hybrid inference](../inference/n5-hybrid.md). That is the homelab's burst
capacity chapter ([#35](https://github.com/Coldaine/coldaine-homelab/issues/35),
[#37](https://github.com/Coldaine/coldaine-homelab/issues/37)) — not an optional footnote.
Invariants bind **now** on the stable set (no etcd, Forgejo, CNPG, or unique durable state on
convertible nodes; platform must remain healthy with every convertible worker absent). Worker VM
and controller automation may lag the Forgejo floor; they must not be designed away.

## Why Talos on the three-node placement subset

Talos is purpose-built for Kubernetes-on-VMs: immutable OS, API-only management, declarative machine
config in git, atomic upgrades with rollback, and a first-class Proxmox install path (custom ISO
with `siderolabs/qemu-guest-agent`, `talosctl gen config`, `talosctl bootstrap`). That matches the
project's git-reproducible, minimal-surface values better than a general-purpose node OS.

The four-member `homelab` Corosync cluster includes `pve-ser8`, but the Kubernetes placement subset
is `pve-ser9`, `pve-ser10`, and `pve-aoostar`. The intended spread is one control-plane VM per member
so a single PVE host failure does not lose Kubernetes quorum. Because the source template uses
non-shared storage, CAPMOX creates replacements on SER10 and the finite placement handoff migrates
them to SER9 and AOOStar with explicit target-storage mappings. CAPMOX rediscovers those moved VMs;
it does not continuously manage their physical placement. Template 9000 uses the common
`x86-64-v3` CPU model because the three hosts have different CPU generations. The AOOStar move can
precede the CAPI pivot; the SER9 move follows seed retirement because seed VM 120 otherwise leaves
insufficient memory for the additional 8 GiB target guest.
`pve-ser8` remains outside this placement set because it carries the radio-coupled Home Assistant
guest. Workloads run on the target control-plane nodes initially; add workers only
on measured need.

At 2026-07-22 verification, the target is `homelab-target-control-plane-57qdk` (VM 100 on SER10),
`homelab-target-control-plane-j6c7p` (VM 101 on SER9), and
`homelab-target-control-plane-9994t` (VM 102 on AOOStar), using addresses `.26`–`.28` and API VIP
`.25`. Template 9000 and each target VM carry a 500 GiB Longhorn disk. VM 101 uses SER9 `vmdata`;
VM 102 uses AOOStar `local-lvm`, whose physical expansion remains an active storage action.
The static seed — `ser9-talos-cp-01` (VM 120 on SER9), `ser10-talos-cp-01` (VM 121 on SER10), and
`aoostar-talos-cp-01` (VM 122 on AOOStar) — is stopped with `onboot=0` after the pivot.

## Networking and ingress

Cilium is the CNI with kube-proxy replacement. Gateway API is the LAN/Tailscale ingress surface.
The stopped seed retains API VIP `.20` and node identities `.21-.23`; the current target uses API
VIP `.25` and node pool `.26-.29`. Cilium LB-IPAM and L2 announcements own
`192.168.30.200-250`, with Forgejo SSH at
`.200` and its HTTPS Gateway at `.201`. A temporary Service established L2 reachability at `.249`
on the seed and was removed. MetalLB is not used.

Service hostnames live under the homelab's owned public domain `moosegoose.xyz`
([network domain](../network/network.md#public-domain)): first `git.moosegoose.xyz`, resolving to
LAN/Tailscale addresses via UDM DNS records. cert-manager issues certificates for Gateway
listeners via ACME DNS-01 against that zone, so clients get publicly trusted certificates with no
inbound exposure and no CA-distribution burden. `external-dns` continuously reconciles
`HTTPRoute` hostnames to DNS records.

### `external-dns-split-horizon`
Status: current
Decision: `external-dns` reconciles Gateway API `HTTPRoute` hostnames using Cloudflare unproxied `A` records (`proxied: false`) pointing to the private gateway IP (`192.168.30.201`) as **Pattern A**. **Pattern B** (using `external-dns-unifi-webhook` to push local DNS directly to the UniFi Gateway at `192.168.30.1`) remains a documented upgrade path if internal hostname privacy on public DNS becomes a requirement.
Why: Reuses existing Doppler `DNS_MOOSEGOOSE_API_TOKEN` without additional infrastructure while preserving `decision:cloudflared-egress-only`.
Revisit when: Internal hostname exposure on public DNS requires zero public leakage, or a local UniFi webhook integration is explicitly deployed.

### `tls-dns01-public-domain`
Status: current
Decision: LAN/Tailscale service TLS uses Let's Encrypt DNS-01 against the owned `moosegoose.xyz` zone as the primary issuer; the internal CA is fallback only. DNS-01 issuance is not WAN exposure — `decision:cloudflared-egress-only` is unchanged.
Why: Publicly trusted certificates remove the need to distribute an internal root to every laptop, agent, and git client, which was an unowned procedure.
Revisit when: The domain lapses, the zone's DNS API becomes unavailable to cert-manager, or a device class cannot reach public DNS during validation.

### `cloudflared-egress-only`
Status: current
Decision: Application and Git remotes are not exposed as WAN inbound listeners; Tailscale and LAN reachability are the default operator paths, and cloudflared is egress-only until an explicit public exposure design is accepted.
Why: The private source-control and household surfaces must not depend on accidental public ingress.
Revisit when: A measured need for public HTTPS or webhook ingress is accepted with its own identity, TLS, and threat model.

### `flat-inter-vlan-trust`
Status: current
Decision: Inter-VLAN reachability that the operator has already established for management (for example Default <-> VLAN 30) is treated as an explicit trust choice for those paths, not as a license to open every VLAN to every workload.
Why: Documented management access must remain usable without collapsing network boundaries for application traffic.
Revisit when: A segmented trust model or zero-trust overlay replaces the current flat management practice.

## Storage

Longhorn provides generic PVCs. Scope is deliberately reduced so Longhorn does not pretend to own
Postgres durability:

- generic PVCs: `numberOfReplicas: 2`
- CNPG database volumes: `numberOfReplicas: 1` (CNPG owns Postgres durability; do not stack
  replication)

CNPG requires live [Garage](../../infra/k8s/platform/garage/README.md) for Barman WAL / PITR before
Forgejo's database is treated as durable. Volume snapshots alone are not enough. Garage replicated
inside the same Longhorn cluster is a fast local target, not an independent disaster copy; a
versioned/off-cluster target and restore proof remain required. PBS restore of guests/PVCs remains a
parallel spike and does not replace the application-aware CNPG path.

### `storage-philosophy`
Status: current
Decision: Cluster storage exists to serve explicit workload classes with matching durability; generic block replication is not a substitute for application-aware database backup and restore.
Why: Stacking Longhorn replicas under CNPG hides failure modes and wastes capacity without improving Postgres recovery.
Revisit when: A workload class needs a different storage product or a measured durability gap appears.

### `longhorn-reduced`
Status: current
Decision: Longhorn runs with reduced replica counts: two for generic PVCs and one for CNPG volumes.
Why: Matches the storage philosophy and keeps the minimal sprint footprint small.
Revisit when: Measured availability needs justify higher generic replica counts or an alternate CSI.

### `cnpg-postgres-home`
Status: current
Decision: CloudNativePG owns all application Postgres; KubeBlocks is not introduced for Postgres.
Why: CNPG is the graduated Postgres operator with volume snapshots, Barman Cloud WAL archiving, and PITR; multi-engine control planes earn a place only after several non-Postgres engines accumulate.
Revisit when: Multiple non-Postgres engines need one unified API and CNPG no longer covers the measured need.

## Secrets

External Secrets Operator (ESO) with a Doppler `ClusterSecretStore` targeting `homelab/dev` is the
in-cluster secret path. Missing secrets fail closed (deploy does not proceed with empty values).
Secret locators that are executable interfaces belong in [access](../access/access.md); secret
values never enter Git. Doppler is authoritative for its workspace — query it directly at
execution time.

### `secrets-single-store`
Status: current
Decision: Doppler `homelab/dev` is the single secret store for platform and application credentials consumed by ESO and operator procedures.
Why: One store avoids split-brain secret ownership between Git, ad-hoc host files, and multiple Doppler configs.
Revisit when: A separate environment boundary is deliberately accepted and issue #11-style splits are redesigned rather than revived ad hoc.

## Home Assistant boundary

Home Assistant remains `haos-01` (VM 111 on SER8), pinned to the SER8 member of the `homelab`
Proxmox cluster while USB radios are host-attached (`decision:home-assistant-sidecar`). The
Kubernetes platform does not host household automation.

### `home-assistant-sidecar`
Status: current
Decision: Home Assistant runs as a dedicated HAOS guest on the Proxmox substrate, not as a Kubernetes workload, while required radios remain host-attached on SER8.
Why: Household operation must survive Kubernetes absence or rebuild; USB radio coupling pins the guest to SER8 until a network-attached redesign is accepted.
Revisit when: Every required device is network-attached and a measured availability need justifies mobility.

## Security revisit cadence

### `security-one-revisit`
Status: current
Decision: Platform security choices (ingress exposure, secret store, mutation paths, TLS) are reconsidered when a new public surface, identity system, or mutation path is introduced — not continuously redesigned in place.
Why: One deliberate revisit beat prevents both neglect and churn while the minimal platform is standing up.
Revisit when: Public cloudflared exposure, OIDC, or additional write-capable automation is accepted.

# Data platform

This document is the accepted target design for the `data-platform` namespace. It records an
execution decision, not current runtime evidence: no workload, endpoint, image build, historical
restore, backup proof, or consumer cutover described here is claimed complete. The ordered work and
its stop conditions are in the [data-platform execution plan](../plans/data-platform-execution.md).

CloudNativePG (CNPG) owns PostgreSQL; FalkorDB owns the separate information-graph requirement.
KubeBlocks is not introduced. Existing `pg-apps` and `soil-db` services coexist until a separately
authorized cleanup, so this design does not rename, replace, or imply deletion of either service.

## Accepted service identities

| Service | Accepted target | Access identity | Data contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pg18-core` | Stable CNPG cluster: two instances, 150 GiB each | `pg18-core-rw.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:5432`; LAN `192.168.30.205:5432` | Custom PostgreSQL 18 image, built remotely with a Shipwright `BuildRun`, then pinned to an immutable GHCR digest. The digest is deliberately not recorded before that build succeeds. |
| `pg19-experimental` | Experimental CNPG cluster: two instances, 50 GiB each | `pg19-experimental-rw.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:5432`; LAN `192.168.30.203:5432` | PostgreSQL 19 Beta 2 standard image, later pinned by immutable digest. It remains a prerelease compatibility lane, not a production default. |
| `falkordb` | One StatefulSet with 20 GiB | `falkordb.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:6379`; LAN `192.168.30.206:6379` | Current pinned FalkorDB image, RDB plus AOF with `appendfsync everysec`. |

There is no `pg18-rw` compatibility alias. Consumers use the declared `pg18-core-rw` name or the
declared LAN endpoint as appropriate to their approved access path.

## Database and graph disposition

| Target | Disposition | Consumer or retained data |
|---|---|---|
| `pg18-core` | Active after coordinated cutover | Forgejo, Soil, MooseGoose, Hangar, `llm_measurements`, `llm_archiver`, `market_live`, and `techdeals_work` |
| `pg18-core` | Restored but unwired | `todo_cards`, `config_fleet`, `cloud_inventory`, and any recoverable non-colliding physical PostgreSQL 18 databases |
| `pg19-experimental` | Active fresh database after coordinated cutover | `coldaine_control_plane`, using the current tasks/approvals/artifacts schema |
| `pg19-experimental` | Restored but unwired | `legacy_control_plane`, retaining the old nodes, edges, claims, evidence, and audit data |
| `falkordb` | Restored before use | The 2026-07-11 RDB; if it is incompatible, use an isolated old-version DUMP/RESTORE conversion rather than overwriting the target casually |

Application repositories retain ownership of schemas, migrations, and application-level
validation. Historical artifacts remain retained until the plan's restore, cutover, and
sole-owner cleanup decisions say otherwise; a successfully restored database is not by itself
wired to a consumer.

## Durability and evidence boundary

The accepted recovery target is [PostgreSQL storage and recovery](../storage/postgresql.md): CNPG
writes each new cluster to a distinct Cloudflare R2 Barman prefix, and FalkorDB writes a scoped
nightly RDB to R2. Longhorn persistence and in-cluster storage do not substitute for that
off-cluster recovery source.

This increment only enrolls data-platform producers into the standing `telemetry-01` boundary:
CNPG on port 9187 and the FalkorDB exporter on port 9121. It creates no telemetry storage stack or
second observability authority.

## Implementation boundary

The target is additive. The prerequisite PostgreSQL recovery change remains PR #97; the PostgreSQL
18 image change follows its merge, and the platform resources, restores, consumer cutover, and
cleanup follow the plan in order. Until their individual evidence exists, service names and IPs in
this document are accepted identities only, not reachable endpoints.

# Data-platform execution

This is the ordered, additive procedure that activates the accepted
[data-platform design](../kubernetes/data-platform.md). It is deliberately not a deployment
record: `data-platform` is not claimed deployed; images are not claimed built or digest-pinned;
endpoints are not claimed reachable; historical restores, consumer cutover, backups, and cleanup
are not claimed complete.

## Ordered gates

1. **Recovery prerequisite — stop before data-platform changes.** Merge [PR #97](https://github.com/Coldaine/coldaine-homelab/pull/97), which establishes the R2 recovery path on its own review boundary. Confirm its merge rather than assuming its manifests or R2 target are live.
2. **PostgreSQL 18 image — stop before platform reconcile.** Rebase the PG18 image work on the merged recovery change, merge its reviewable PR, run the remote Shipwright `BuildRun`, and record the resulting immutable GHCR digest in the accepted deployment input. Do not invent or use a mutable tag as the digest.
3. **Additive platform activation — stop on any failed reconciliation.** Merge and reconcile the data-platform resources: both CNPG clusters, FalkorDB, declared services/LAN identities, ExternalSecret inputs, and producer-only telemetry enrollment. Verify each intended workload and endpoint from its normal access path. Do not remove `pg-apps` or `soil-db` in this phase.
4. **Historical recovery — stop on incompatible or baseline-mismatched data.** Restore the stated PostgreSQL catalogue and the FalkorDB 2026-07-11 RDB into the designated wired or unwired targets. If the RDB is incompatible, perform the isolated old-version DUMP/RESTORE conversion. Preserve source artifacts and keep restored-but-unwired databases disconnected from consumers.
5. **Coordinated consumer cutover — stop and roll back to the prior approved consumer path on a failed migration, validation, or normal-path connection.** Move only the declared active consumers, verify their repository-owned migrations and application workflows, and keep `legacy_control_plane` unwired. Endpoint availability is not sufficient acceptance.
6. **New-target recovery proof and sole-owner cleanup — stop before deletion if backup or recovery evidence is missing.** Prove the new CNPG R2 backup/PITR path and FalkorDB nightly RDB path, then make each cleanup decision explicitly. Current source backups block destructive cleanup, not platform activation or an otherwise successful cutover.

## Completion conditions

This plan may be deleted only after the lasting design remains in Kubernetes and storage
authorities, each intended consumer has its appropriate cutover evidence, the required off-cluster
recovery paths are proven, and all former owners are either intentionally retained or separately
cleaned up. A merged manifest PR, a running pod, or an answering endpoint alone does not meet those
conditions.

# PostgreSQL storage and recovery

This document records the accepted recovery design for the new data platform. It is not evidence
that the R2 paths, backups, restores, or consumer cutovers are operating. The ordered activation
and proof gates are in the [data-platform execution plan](../plans/data-platform-execution.md).

## Off-cluster recovery authority

Each new CNPG cluster (`pg18-core` and `pg19-experimental`) uses its own Barman prefix in
Cloudflare R2. Continuous WAL and base backups retain a seven-day recovery window; a fourteen-day
R2 hard-expiry lifecycle is the outer retention boundary. FalkorDB writes a scoped nightly RDB to
R2 with the same fourteen-day hard expiry. The exact R2 credentials and their delivery remain
runtime concerns; secret values do not enter this repository.

The R2 destination must survive the Kubernetes, Longhorn, and database-runtime failure domain.
Longhorn volumes and snapshots can support same-cluster recovery but are not independent database
backups. Garage is not the recovery authority for these new PostgreSQL clusters, and PBS guest/PVC
recovery does not replace application-aware PostgreSQL restore or point-in-time recovery.

## Recovery and cleanup boundary

Current preserved artifacts remain source evidence while the new targets are built and historical
data is assessed. They are a prerequisite for destructive cleanup, not a gate against the approved
platform deployment or a reason to block coordinated cutover once the applicable restore and
consumer validation gates pass.

New-target backup success is required before sole-owner cleanup. It is not, by itself, a cutover
gate: each consumer moves only after its data baseline, migration/validation, normal access path,
and coordinated rollback boundary are proven. `legacy_control_plane` remains retained and unwired
until its separate owner/disposition decision; it must not be discarded as an obsolete pre-release
artifact.

The target service identities and database catalogue are authoritative in
[data platform](../kubernetes/data-platform.md). The recovery operation remains unfinished and is
authoritative in the [data-platform execution plan](../plans/data-platform-execution.md).

# Justfile Tooling Design Philosophy

This document records the architectural design philosophy for repository-level CLI task automation via `justfile` in `coldaine-homelab`. It details how `just` serves as an audited, high-density interface for both human operators and AI agents (such as Antigravity, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor).

---

## 1. Core Purpose & Context

In a homelab and application platform codebase, operators and AI agents routinely perform cross-cutting CLI tasks: configuring cluster credentials, validating Kubernetes manifests, running documentation linters, and triggering GitOps reconciliations.

Without a standardized task runner, human operators and AI agents are forced to write multi-line, error-prone shell boilerplate (e.g. verbose `doppler run --` wrappers, complex string escaping, or hardcoded IP addresses). 

The `justfile` provides a **thin, self-documenting, and deterministic dispatch layer** that standardizes these workflows without introducing heavy frameworks or external runtime dependencies.

---

## 2. Design Principles

### Principle 1: Judicious & Minimal (Thin Dispatcher)
The `justfile` is **not** a dumping ground for long shell scripts or transient, single-sprint hacks.
- **5 to 8 Enduring Verbs**: Only include recipes that are reusable across any task or sprint (e.g., `setup`, `validate`, `d`, `pve`, `flux-sync`).
- **Delegate Complex Logic**: If a task requires complex branching, multi-step error handling, or custom logic, place it in a dedicated file under `scripts/` or `tools/` and call it from the `justfile`.

### Principle 2: Zero Hardcoded Infrastructure State
Infrastructure state (Proxmox guest IDs, node IPs, network leases, and secret tokens) is dynamic.
- **Dynamic Resolution**: Recipes must never hardcode single-use VM IDs (e.g., `qm guest exec 111`), static 6-IP ping lists, or inline base64 secret decoders.
- **Authoritative Integration**: Recipes delegate state to live authorities: Doppler for secrets (`KUBECONFIG_HOMELAB_TARGET` and `TALOSCONFIG_HOMELAB_TARGET`), `talosctl` for node management, and Kustomize/Flux for manifest declarations.

### Principle 3: Agent-Human Equivalence & High Token Density
AI agents and human operators interact with the repository through the same canonical interface.
- **High Token Efficiency**: Running `just --list` returns 100% of the repository's operational capabilities in under ~100 tokens, eliminating the need for an AI agent to parse hundreds of lines of shell scripts.
- **Zero Shell Hallucination**: Exposing standard verbs prevents AI agents from guessing invalid CLI flags, breaking subshell quoting on Windows/Linux, or attempting to connect to retired cluster IP addresses.

### Principle 4: Cross-Platform Subshell Execution
Operators work on Windows (`pwsh`), while containerized agents and CI run on Linux (`bash`).
- **Explicit Shell Binding**: The `justfile` specifies shell execution explicitly (`pwsh` on Windows) to guarantee that commands behave identically inside interactive terminals and non-interactive agent subprocesses.

---

## 3. Standardized Recipe Catalog

| Recipe | Function | Rationale & Problem Solved |
|---|---|---|
| `just setup` | Syncs `KUBECONFIG_HOMELAB_TARGET` and `TALOSCONFIG_HOMELAB_TARGET` from Doppler (`homelab/dev`) into `$HOME\.kube\config` and `$HOME\.talos\config` | Prevents connection timeouts caused by workstation/agent `kubeconfig` pointing to stale or retired seed cluster IPs (`.20`). |
| `just validate` | Runs `kustomize build infra/k8s/platform \| Out-Null` | Verifies that all Kubernetes platform manifests render without YAML or CRD schema errors. |
| `just d *cmd` | Executes any command wrapped in Doppler secrets (`doppler run --project homelab --config dev -- ...`) | Eliminates typing verbose Doppler project/config flags and multi-layer string escaping. |
| `just pve *cmd` | Executes remote SSH commands on PVE cluster seed host `192.168.30.7` (SER10) | Provides quick hypervisor inspection without writing multi-line SSH environment variables. |
| `just flux-sync` | Triggers Flux reconciliation (`flux reconcile kustomization target-platform --with-source`) | Forces immediate in-cluster reconciliation after merging GitOps pull requests. |

---

## 4. Anti-Patterns Explicitly Rejected

1. **Hardcoding VMIDs or Node IP Lists**: Single-sprint scripts (e.g., `ssh root@192.168.30.2 "qm guest exec 111 -- ha ..."`) are rejected. Transient VM operations belong in live debugging sessions, not root `justfiles`.
2. **In-Line Base64 Secret Decoders**: Extracting base64 secrets from `kubectl` is an anti-pattern. Doppler and External Secrets Operator (ESO) are the single source of truth for secret management.
3. **Monolithic "God Tasks"**: Recipes must remain granular. Combining linting, building, deploying, and testing into a single giant target obscures failure diagnosis for agents and humans alike.

---

## 5. Related Documentation & Authority

- [NORTH_STAR.md](../NORTH_STAR.md) — Enduring outcomes and foundational control rules.
- [DOC_GUIDE.md](../DOC_GUIDE.md) — Documentation placement, link integrity, and maintenance rules.
- [access.md](../access/access.md) — Non-secret client access paths and credential locators (`KUBECONFIG_HOMELAB_TARGET`, `TALOSCONFIG_HOMELAB_TARGET`).
- [kubernetes.md](../kubernetes/kubernetes.md) — Kubernetes platform desired state, VIP reservations (`192.168.30.25`), and node pool addressing.

# Doppler

## Critical Trigger

You must load this skill before any action involving secrets: API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, `.env` files, service tokens, OAuth credentials, webhook secrets, cloud credentials, signed URLs, cookies, auth headers, or environment variables that may carry credentials.

If unsure whether a value is a secret, treat it as a secret. Keep secret values out of chat, logs, diffs, committed files, and durable docs.

Use Doppler as a secrets injection layer. Prefer CLI-driven environment injection (`doppler run -- ...`) over in-process SDK calls, vault enumeration, or committed secret files.

## Operating Rules

- Do not print secret values into transcripts unless the user explicitly asks for the value.
- Prefer storing application and workstation secrets in Doppler. CI and production systems should store only the scoped `DOPPLER_TOKEN` or platform-required bootstrap credential.
- Document secret names, projects/configs, and injection commands; do not document secret values or one-off local token state.
- Prefer names-only or boolean checks: `doppler secrets --only-names`, `test -n "$VAR"`, or PowerShell `if ($env:VAR)`.
- Do not commit `.env`, downloaded secret exports, service tokens, fallback files, or rendered config files containing credentials.
- Use service tokens only in CI/production secret stores, never in repo files.
- Treat `doppler.yaml` as safe repo configuration: it names project/config only.
- Use `doppler run -- ...` for normal application execution. Application code should read ordinary environment variables.
- Use `doppler run --mount ...` when an application must read a secret file; prefer environment injection for normal command execution.
- Avoid `--preserve-env` for secrets unless there is a deliberate reason to let pre-existing shell values override Doppler.
- Use `--silent` for destructive secret-management commands where possible; some CLI versions print a secrets table after mutation.
- Do not use bare configuration display, its `--all` variant, or the configuration debug subcommand in an agent transcript. Those views include token fields, and the debug form may reveal the saved CLI token. Query only known non-secret options explicitly.
- For current command syntax, verify with `doppler --version` and `doppler <command> --help` before changing scripts or docs.

## Core Model

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Workplace | Top-level Doppler organization |
| Project | Secret namespace for an app, service, or shared secret group |
| Config | Environment within a project, such as `dev`, `stg`, or `prd` |
| Secret | Key-value pair injected into child processes |
| Service token | Revocable token scoped to a project/config for CI or production |
| CLI token | Developer login token saved by `doppler login` |

Resolution order for most CLI commands is service token, explicit flags, local scoped config, then parent scoped config.

## Quick Start

Install:

```shell
# Windows
winget install doppler

# macOS
brew install dopplerhq/cli/doppler

# Linux / CI
(curl -Ls --tlsv1.2 --proto "=https" --retry 3 https://cli.doppler.com/install.sh || wget -t 3 -qO- https://cli.doppler.com/install.sh) | sh
```

Set up a repo:

```shell
doppler login
doppler setup -p my-project -c dev
doppler run -- python app.py
```

Commit a team setup file:

```yaml
setup:
  project: my-project
  config: dev

flags:
  analytics: false
  env-warning: false
  update-check: false
```

Then teammates can run:

```shell
doppler setup --no-interactive
doppler run -- your-command
```

## Running Commands

POSIX shells:

```shell
doppler run -- uv run pytest
doppler run -p my-project -c dev -- ./scripts/test.sh
doppler run --command './configure && ./process-jobs'
```

PowerShell:

```powershell
doppler run -- uv run pytest
doppler run -p my-project -c dev -- powershell -NoProfile -File .\scripts\test.ps1
doppler run --command "uv run pytest"
```

Use `--command` for shell operators, pipelines, and command strings. Use `-- ...` for normal argv forwarding.

## Safe Diagnostics

Check active config:

```shell
doppler configure get project config --plain
doppler me
doppler secrets --only-names
```

Check whether a secret is injected without printing the value:

```shell
doppler run -- sh -c 'test -n "$DATABASE_URL" && echo DATABASE_URL=set || echo DATABASE_URL=missing'
```

```powershell
doppler run -- powershell -NoProfile -Command "if ($env:DATABASE_URL) { 'DATABASE_URL=set' } else { 'DATABASE_URL=missing' }"
```

Only use raw value commands for intentional secret handling:

```shell
doppler secrets get SECRET_NAME --plain
```

## Adding Secrets

```shell
doppler secrets set API_KEY value
printf '%s' "$CERT_CONTENTS" | doppler secrets set CERT_PEM
doppler secrets upload secrets.env
```

PowerShell:

```powershell
doppler secrets set API_KEY value
Get-Content -Raw .\cert.pem | doppler secrets set CERT_PEM
doppler secrets upload .\secrets.env
```

Prefer piping multiline values instead of pasting them into shell history.

## CI And Production

Create one service token per project/config and store it in the CI provider's secret store as `DOPPLER_TOKEN`:

```shell
doppler configs tokens create -p my-project -c prd ci-token --plain
```

GitHub Actions pattern:

```yaml
- name: Install Doppler CLI
  run: (curl -Ls --tlsv1.2 --proto "=https" --retry 3 https://cli.doppler.com/install.sh || wget -t 3 -qO- https://cli.doppler.com/install.sh) | sh
- name: Run tests
  run: doppler run -- uv run pytest
  env:
    DOPPLER_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DOPPLER_TOKEN }}
```

Service token project/config takes precedence over `doppler setup` and `-p`/`-c` flags.

## Fallback Files

Doppler may write encrypted fallback/cache files under the configured Doppler directory. Use them for availability, not as repo artifacts.

```shell
doppler run --fallback-only -- ./start.sh
doppler run --no-fallback -- ./start.sh
doppler run clean --dry-run
```

If a fallback must move between build and deploy stages, use a dedicated passphrase from the CI secret store, not a literal in YAML:

```shell
doppler secrets download --passphrase "$DOPPLER_FALLBACK_PASSPHRASE" -p my-project -c prd
doppler run --fallback ./doppler.json --passphrase "$DOPPLER_FALLBACK_PASSPHRASE" -- ./start.sh
```

## Mounting Secrets

`doppler run --mount ...` exposes secrets through an ephemeral mounted file path and does not inject the secrets into the environment. The path is available as `DOPPLER_CLI_SECRETS_PATH`.

```shell
doppler run --mount secrets.json -- cat secrets.json
doppler run --mount .env --format env -- ./start.sh
doppler run --mount config.yml --mount-template config.yml.tmpl -- ./start.sh
```

Some frameworks reject named pipes or ephemeral files. If that happens, use environment injection with plain `doppler run -- ...`.

## References

Load these only when needed:

- [references/commands.md](references/commands.md): command reference, platform notes, and troubleshooting.
- [references/ci-fallbacks.md](references/ci-fallbacks.md): CI, service tokens, fallback files, and Docker patterns.

## Review Checklist

Before promoting or committing Doppler work:

- `doppler --version`
- `doppler configure get project config --plain`
- `doppler me`
- `doppler secrets --only-names`
- Run the target command through `doppler run -- ...`
- Confirm no secret values were added to files, logs, diffs, or transcripts.

## Learnings

### 2026-06-29

#### What Worked
- Reuse one **classic** GitHub PAT (`GHCR_BUILD_TOKEN`) for both GHCR push (`kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` → `ghcr-push`) and Shipwright private-repo clone (`kubernetes.io/basic-auth` → `git-clone`). No separate `GITHUB_CLONE_TOKEN` if the PAT has `repo` + `write:packages`.
- Boolean Doppler checks without printing values: `doppler secrets get KEY -p PROJECT -c CONFIG --plain 2>$null` then test `$LASTEXITCODE` and `[string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($v)` / `$v.Length` — never echo the value.
- `doppler secrets --only-names` across projects to reconcile manifest `remoteRef.key` names vs vault (e.g. `LLM_ARCHIVAL_DB_PASSWORD` vs `LLMARCHIVER_DB_PASSWORD`).
- Audit scripts must call seed/bootstrap helpers with **read-only** flags (`-ReadOnly`); audits that invoke writers mutate production state.

#### What Failed
- Assuming credentials are missing before a Doppler names/existence audit — many keys already existed under `databases/dev` or `coldaine-k8s/dev_homelab`.
- Fine-grained GitHub PAT UI for GHCR — **no** `write:packages` under per-repo permissions; use a **classic** PAT for `ghcr.io` push.
- Treating `SOPS_AGE_KEY` as the age decrypt key when it was truncated; use `AGE_PRIVATE_KEY` when present and valid (`StartsWith('AGE-SECRET-KEY')`).

#### Configuration Notes
- ESO `ClusterSecretStore` only sees secrets in the **service token's** Doppler project/config. Keys in other projects (e.g. `secrets_managment/dev` for Proxmox, `databases/dev` for legacy names) require token scope alignment or manifest key migration to the cluster project (`coldaine-k8s/dev_homelab`).
- Shipwright git clone failure (`could not read Username for 'https://github.com'`) is usually missing `spec.source.git.cloneSecret`, not a missing Doppler key — check wiring before creating new keys.
- If user pastes a token in chat: store via `doppler secrets set ... --silent`, verify ESO sync, warn about rotation — do not repeat the token in the response.

# PDM CLI Operations

Use `proxmox-datacenter-manager-client` as the shared process interface for agents and operators. An environment may expose a small launcher around that binary for credential retrieval and TLS pinning. It connects to the standing PDM API; it is not another service, database, MCP server, or source of truth.

The official client currently requires a compatible amd64 Debian environment, network access to a same-major PDM server, and a secret-safe credential command.

## Operating Contract

- Load `$doppler` before handling authentication in a Doppler-backed environment; otherwise load the applicable secrets-management skill.
- Resolve the PDM endpoint, TLS fingerprint, non-secret auth ID, and target names from the environment's canonical operational repository. Never copy that inventory into this skill.
- Use the identity supplied by the environment. A read-only identity is suitable for inspection or qualification, not for an authorized execution task; do not silently downgrade the requested operation.
- Verify the client and PDM share the same major version before relying on it.
- Prefer the environment-owned launcher when one exists. It must still invoke the official client and preserve its output and exit code.
- The raw client requires `login` before ordinary commands; persist its XDG ticket cache. Pass the password only to `login` through `--password-command` or a protected short-lived `--password-file`.
- Never place a password in argv, a committed file, a prompt, or durable output.
- Pin the expected TLS certificate and never suppress verification. PDM client 1.1.6 does not seed its verifier cache from `--fingerprint` during noninteractive login; use the independently verified cache-pin procedure in the reference or a launcher that implements it.
- Request `--output-format json` for agent work. Preserve the original output when evidence matters; client 1.1.6 emits a non-JSON terminal `TaskStatus` for some mutations even when JSON was requested.
- Start with `remote list`, then select the exact remote, node, and guest. A VMID is not globally meaningful without its remote.
- Read current state immediately before a mutation. Stay within the task's authority while diagnosing and resolving proven dependencies needed to complete it.
- Treat an accepted request or returned UPID as started, not completed. Require terminal `stopped` plus `exitstatus=OK`, then read state again.
- Distinguish client/authentication failure, PDM unavailability, remote unavailability, and an unsuccessful remote task. Report the actual boundary.
- PDM is the normal fleet surface. Native PVE or PBS access remains the explicit break-glass path when PDM is unavailable; do not deploy a parallel control plane as a workaround.

## Workflow

1. Read the owning repository's current access and fleet references.
2. Confirm the binary exists and record `--version` or package version without changing the host.
3. Select the environment launcher or build the two-step raw-client login using the endpoint, user ID, TLS pin, persistent XDG state, and a secret-safe password source.
4. Prove authentication with `remote list` and JSON output.
5. Read pre-state and select the exact remote, node, resource ID, and name.
6. For a mutation, confirm the supplied identity has the necessary authority, execute the exact action once, follow its task to success or failure, and verify post-state.
7. Return concise evidence: PDM endpoint identity, remote, node, guest ID and name when applicable, action, UPID or synchronous result, and final state. Redact credentials.

## Command Reference

Read [references/commands.md](references/commands.md) for installation boundaries, invocation templates, discovery commands, task follow-through, and mutation safeguards. Verify live syntax with `help --verbose` before using a command that is not covered there.

1-# Documentation and issue-workflow guide
2-
3:This guide decides where knowledge belongs and how it moves. It is the authority for documentation placement, retrieval, and issue-to-doc workflow.
4-
5-## Core rules
6-
7:- Use the document or live system authoritative for the truth.
8:- Write each durable fact once in the smallest authoritative surface that needs it.
9-- Expand or split documentation when a focused document is independently useful.
10-- Do not force the repository into a fixed four-kinds model or a fewer-docs rule if that would hide useful distinctions.
11-- Authority belongs to documents and live systems, not to people, teams, hosts, VMs, or containers.
12-- Progressive disclosure is the default: broad surfaces route to narrower ones when that improves retrieval.
--
15-## Documentation surfaces
16-
17-### Architecture
18-
19:Architecture is authoritative for homelab-wide relationships: topology, layer boundaries, failure
20-and recovery boundaries, control boundaries, evidence boundaries, and other cross-domain decisions
21-that matter beyond one domain. Keep it broad. Do not use Architecture to restate detailed
22-implementation facts that belong elsewhere.
23-
24-### Capability Map
25-
26:The Capability Map is the current-state registry for capabilities and their authoritative documents.
27-It is a routing surface, not a guest inventory, issue queue, deployment log, or narrative essay. Use
28:it to answer what capability exists, what state it is in, and which document is authoritative for
29-the detail.
30-
31-### Domain overview
32-
33:Each domain overview is the root document for one domain folder. It states its authoritative scope,
34-records durable domain facts and accepted design, and routes to focused design, deployment,
35:procedure, or recovery documents that are useful on their own. A domain overview may also route to
36-active plans when work is unfinished.
37-
38-### Focused documents
39-
40:Create a focused document when a subject is large enough, changes on a different cadence, serves a different audience, or benefits from separate recovery or deployment discovery. Examples include design, deployment, procedure, recovery, bootstrap, and migration docs. A focused document is valid only when it makes retrieval or maintenance easier; otherwise keep the material in the domain overview. Do not duplicate the same durable fact across multiple surfaces.
41-
42-### Active plans
43-
44-Plans are for unfinished work only. They record remaining work, gates, and acceptance criteria, plus any bounded execution detail that does not yet belong in a durable domain document. Plans are deleted when the work lands and their lasting results have been recorded elsewhere. Do not keep completed plans as archives or status reports.
--
47-
48-Live state is read from the system, not frozen into Markdown. Examples include power state,
49-running/stopped state, free space, queue depth, negotiated rates, current health, progress counters,
50-and other right-now measurements. If the state is transient, use the live source. If it becomes
51:durable, record it in the authoritative document.
52-
53-### Issue, PR, and Git history
54-
55:Issues, pull requests, and Git history record chronology, discussion, and review evidence. They preserve what changed, why it changed, and how it was validated, but they do not replace the current authoritative document for the truth itself.
56-
57-## Placement and expansion rules
58-
59-- Write a fact once in the document whose purpose requires it.
60:- If a fact already belongs in an authoritative document, update that document instead of creating another source of truth.
61-- Add a new focused document when the topic is independently useful or when splitting it reduces ambiguity without losing retrieval.
62-- Add a new domain only when a new durable capability or standing service is accepted; do not create domains speculatively.
63:- Keep every document reachable by link from a root document, the Capability Map, or its domain overview. No orphans.
64-- Reject any rule that says the repository must always collapse to a smaller fixed set of categories or documents. Use the amount of structure that makes the truth easier to find and safer to change.
65-
66-## Documentation impact assessment
67-
68-Every change to code, deployment inputs, tooling, configuration, or infrastructure requires a documentation impact assessment.
69-
70-1. Identify the durable truth the change affects, if any.
71:2. Name the document or live system authoritative for that truth.
72-3. Decide whether the change alters architecture, accepted design, current implementation facts, standing procedure, recovery, capability state, or a safety boundary.
73:4. If durable truth changed, update the affected authoritative documents in the same pull request.
74-5. If durable truth did not change, explain why in the pull request instead of manufacturing a Markdown change.
75-
76-Do not require ADRs, mandatory metadata blocks, blast-radius forms, rejected-alternatives sections, or revisit triggers for every decision. Add that context only when it materially prevents a likely mistake.
77-
78-## Selective persistence and identity
79-
80-Persist only what would be dangerous or incorrect to forget and that cannot be reliably recovered live. Prefer durable identities, boundaries, recovery paths, constraints, and decisions over transient measurements or routine status.
81-
82:When prose refers to Proxmox guests, use human-readable identity: name plus kind plus ID plus relevant authority, for example `pdm-01` (VM 200 on SER10), `haos-01` (VM 111 on SER8), or `n5-llm-01` (CT 300 on N5). Include the authority when placement matters.
83-
84-## Issue intake and triage
85-
86-GitHub Issues are unclassified intake. They should describe the need, affected systems, desired observable outcome, constraints, and sanitized evidence.
87-
88-During triage:
89-
90:- determine which capability and document are authoritative for the outcome;
91-- link the issue to that capability row and document;
92-- if the issue introduces a durable role, add or update the capability map entry and write accepted design before treating implementation as current;
93-- put unfinished implementation into a plan with observable acceptance; and
94-- keep the issue focused on coordination rather than architecture or completion claims.
95-
96-Close an issue only when its stated observable outcome and every acceptance condition are satisfied.
97:The closing comment should point to the current authoritative documents, the verification performed,
98-the final state, and any deliberately excluded work.
99-
100-## Plan lifecycle
101-
102-A plan is a temporary work surface for unfinished change.
103-
104-- A plan records what remains, how to know it is done, and any bounded execution detail that does not yet belong in a durable document.
105:- A plan does not track progress as a status dashboard and does not replace the authoritative domain document.
106:- When the work lands, move lasting results to the authoritative document, update the Capability Map
107-  if the capability state changed, and delete the plan in the same change.
108-- Do not keep completed plans as archives, changelogs, or session reports. Git, issues, and PRs already preserve chronology.
109-
110-## Secrets and access
111-
112-Never commit a password, private key, token, auth key, recovery code, or other secret value.
113-
114:Record client-side paths, pinned host identities, and dated authentication evidence in [access](access/access.md). Doppler is authoritative for its workspace, secret names, values, consumers, and rotation state; query it directly at execution time. Do not create repository inventories, snapshots, locator catalogs, or mappings of Doppler contents. An exact secret name belongs in Git only when it is an executable interface consumed by code or configuration.
115-
116-Do not confuse a secret with the non-secret identity that selects it. User IDs, realms, token IDs,
117-certificate fingerprints, roles, scopes, and rotation procedures are operational state; record each
118:once in its authoritative document without the secret value.
119-
120-## No session reports
121-
122:Do not create dated session reports or similar retrospective work logs. Use the current authoritative document for the durable truth and issue, PR, or Git history for chronology.

# GitHub PR Comment Handler

Use this skill when the user wants to work through requested changes on a GitHub pull request. Use the GitHub app from this plugin for PR metadata and patch context, but treat thread-aware review data as a `gh api graphql` problem because the connector comment surface is flat and does not preserve full review-thread state.

Run all `gh` commands with elevated network access. If CLI auth is required, confirm `gh auth status` first and ask the user to authenticate with `gh auth login` if it fails.

## Workflow

1. Resolve the PR.
   - If the user provides a repository and PR number or URL, use that directly.
   - If the request is about the current branch PR, use local git context plus `gh auth status` and `gh pr view --json number,url` to resolve it.
2. Inspect review context with thread-aware reads.
   - Use the GitHub app from this plugin to fetch PR metadata and patch context when the repo and PR are known.
   - Use the bundled `scripts/fetch_comments.py` workflow whenever the task depends on unresolved review threads, inline review locations, or resolution state. That script fetches `reviewThreads`, `isResolved`, `isOutdated`, and file and line anchors that the connector comment surface does not preserve.
   - Use connector-only comment reads only for lightweight top-level PR comment summaries.
3. Cluster actionable review threads.
   - Group comments by file or behavior area.
   - Separate actionable change requests from informational comments, approvals, already-resolved threads, and duplicates.
4. Confirm scope before editing.
   - Present numbered actionable threads with a one-line summary of the required change.
   - If the user did not ask to fix everything, ask which threads to address.
   - If the user asks to fix everything, interpret that as all unresolved actionable threads and call out anything ambiguous.

# GitHub

## Overview

Use this skill as the umbrella entrypoint for general GitHub work in this plugin. It should decide whether the task stays in repo and PR triage or should be handed off to a more specific review, CI, or publish workflow.

This plugin is intentionally hybrid:

- Prefer the GitHub app from this plugin for repository, issue, pull request, comment, label, reaction, and PR creation workflows.
- Use local `git` and `gh` only when the connector does not cover the job well, especially for current-branch PR discovery, branch creation, commit and push, `gh auth status`, and GitHub Actions log inspection.
- Keep connector state and local checkout context aligned. If the request is about the current branch, resolve the local repo and branch before acting.

Once the intent is clear, route to the specialist skill immediately and do not keep broad GitHub triage in scope longer than needed.

## Connector-First Responsibilities

Handle these directly in this skill when the request does not need a narrower specialist workflow:

- repository orientation once the repo, PR, issue, or local checkout is identified
- recent PR or issue triage
- PR metadata summaries
- PR patch inspection
- PR comments, labels, and reactions
- issue lookup and summarization
- PR creation after a branch is already pushed

Prefer the GitHub app from this plugin for those flows because it provides structured PR, issue, and review-adjacent data without depending on a local checkout. If the repository is not already identifiable from the user request or local git context, ask for the repo instead of pretending there is a repo-search flow that may not exist.

## Routing Rules

1. Resolve the operating context first:
   - If the user provides a repository, PR number, issue number, or URL, use that.
   - If the request is about "this branch" or "the current PR", resolve local git context and use `gh` only as needed to discover the branch PR.
   - If the repository is still ambiguous after local inspection, ask for the repo identifier.
2. Classify the request before taking action:
   - `repo or PR triage`: summarize PRs, issues, patches, comments, labels, reactions, or repository state
   - `review follow-up`: unresolved review threads, requested changes, or inline review feedback
   - `CI debugging`: failing checks, Actions logs, or CI root-cause analysis
   - `publish changes`: create or switch branches, stage changes, commit, push, and open a draft PR
3. Route to the specialist skill as soon as the category is clear:
   - Review comments and requested changes: `../gh-address-comments/SKILL.md`
   - Failing GitHub Actions checks: `../gh-fix-ci/SKILL.md`
   - Commit, push, and open PR: `../yeet/SKILL.md`
4. Keep the hybrid model consistent after routing:
   - connector first for PR and issue data
   - local `git` and `gh` only for the specific gaps the connector does not cover

## Default Workflow

1. Resolve repository and item scope.
2. Gather structured PR or issue context through the GitHub app from this plugin.
3. Decide whether the task stays in connector-backed triage or needs a specialist skill.
4. Route immediately when the work becomes review follow-up, CI debugging, or publish workflow.
5. End with a clear summary of what was inspected, what changed, and what remains.

## Output Expectations

- For triage requests, return a concise summary of the repository, PR, or issue state and the next likely action.
- For mixed requests, tell the user which specialist path you are taking and why.
- For connector-backed write actions, restate the exact PR, issue, label, or reaction target before applying the change.
- Never imply that GitHub Actions logs are available through the connector alone. That remains a `gh` workflow.

## Examples

- "Use GitHub to summarize the open PRs in this repo and tell me what needs attention."
- "Help with this PR."
- "Review the latest comments on PR 482 and tell me what is actionable."
- "Debug the failing checks on this branch."
- "Commit these changes, push them, and open a draft PR."

+This ledger records the interface each consumer must exercise during cutover. It is an interface

+| LLM measurements | `LocalLargeLanguageModels` | Historical `pg18`/LAN path | `pg18-core-rw.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:5432`, database `llm_measurements`; `LLM_MEASUREMENTS_DSN` | Read existing measurement rows and insert a bounded normal measurement record |

+| Hangar | Hangar consumer repository / owner to be confirmed from its current checkout | Historical source to be inventoried before cutover | `pg18-core-rw.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:5432`, database `hangar`; connection variable remains consumer-owned until verified | Repository-specific normal read/write path and row-baseline comparison |
+| TechDeals | `TechdealsHandoff` / TechDeals consumer owner | Historical source to be inventoried before cutover | `pg18-core-rw.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:5432`, database `techdeals_work` | Repository-specific normal read/write path and row-baseline comparison |

  ```mermaid
          end

          MW3["Primary merges/reconciles reviewed connection changes"]
          MW4["Resume reconciliation and restart consumers in parallel"]
          MW5["Each agent exercises its consumer's ordinary read/write path"]
          MW6["Maintenance window ends"]

          MW1 --> MW2
          MW2 --> F1
          MW2 --> S1
          MW2 --> O1
          F3 --> MW3
          S3 --> MW3
          O1 --> MW3
          MW3 --> MW4 --> MW5 --> MW6
      end

      READY --> MW1

      subgraph W4["Parallel completion tail"]
          direction LR
          V1["Agent A · Confirm new PG base backups and WAL objects"]
          V2["Agent B · Confirm current FalkorDB RDB object"]
          V3["Agent C · Finalize consumer and recovery documentation"]
          V4["Primary · Refresh live cleanup inventory"]
          V5["Primary · Update only current-state documents and capability rows that changed"]
      end
  ```

  The serialized critical path is only:

  ```text
  PR #97 merge
  → image branch rebase
  → image PR merge
  → remote BuildRun
  → immutable PG18 digest
  → additive platform PR merge
  → new services reconcile
  → historical restores
  → coordinated current-data cutover
  → new backups exist
  → old-source cleanup
  ```

  Archive analysis, platform authoring, recovery tooling, consumer changes, documentation drafting, secret wiring, cleanup inventory, and
  telemetry preparation run alongside that path.

  ## Agent ownership

  | Execution period | Agent A | Agent B | Agent C | Primary |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Wave 1 | PR #97 and current-source backups | PG18 image PR | Platform manifests and recovery tooling | Catalog, consumer map, shared
  integration |
  | Wave 2 | Backup inventory and PG18 restore tooling | Consumer PR groups | Final platform commits | Review, improve, rebase, publish platform
  PR |
  | Wave 3 | PG18 historical recovery | PG19 active and legacy recovery | FalkorDB recovery | Consumer integration and live coordination |
  | Cutover | Forgejo pipeline | Soil pipeline | Remaining consumers | Stop/start coordination and shared config merge |
  | Completion | PostgreSQL backup facts | FalkorDB backup fact | Durable documentation | Cleanup inventory, final integration, PR publication |

  Agents receive exclusive directory or repository ownership. The primary alone edits shared aggregation files such as platform Kustomizations
  and cross-domain routing documents.

  ## Locked platform shape

  - Namespace: `data-platform`.
  - Stable cluster: `pg18-core`, two instances, 150 GiB each.
  - Experimental cluster: `pg19-experimental`, two instances, 50 GiB each, official PostgreSQL 19 Beta 2 standard image pinned by digest.
  PostgreSQL 19 remains pre-release. [PostgreSQL 19 status](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/19/release-19.html)
  - FalkorDB: one 20 GiB StatefulSet using the current pinned server image.
  - No KubeBlocks installation.
  - Existing `pg-apps` and `soil-db` coexist until cleanup.
  - The PG18 platform PR consumes the image digest returned by the merged image BuildRun; no unresolved tag reaches review.

  Canonical endpoints:

  | Service | Internal | LAN |
  |---|---|---|
  | PG18 | `pg18-core-rw.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:5432` | `192.168.30.205:5432` |
  | PG19 | `pg19-experimental-rw.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:5432` | `192.168.30.203:5432` |
  | FalkorDB | `falkordb.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:6379` | `192.168.30.206:6379` |

  No permanent `pg18-rw` compatibility alias is introduced.

  ## Recovery placement

  `pg18-core` active/wired:

  - `forgejo`
  - `soil`
  - `moosegoose`
  - `hangar`
  - `llm_measurements`
  - `llm_archiver`
  - `market_live`
  - `techdeals_work`

  `pg18-core` restored but unwired:

  - `todo_cards`
  - `config_fleet`
  - `cloud_inventory`
  - Any additional recoverable database discovered in the physical PG18 copy, using its original name unless that collides with an active
  database.

  `pg19-experimental`:

  - `coldaine_control_plane`: fresh current schema, active and wired.
  - `legacy_control_plane`: old `nodes`, `edges`, `claims`, evidence, and audit data, restored but unwired.

  FalkorDB:

  - Restore the 2026-07-11 RDB.
  - If the current image cannot read it, perform conversion in an isolated old-version pod and move graph values with `DUMP`/`RESTORE`.
  - Active service uses RDB plus AOF with `appendfsync everysec`. [FalkorDB durability](https://docs.falkordb.com/operations/durability)

  ## Backup and telemetry work

  - PR #97 retains the already-decided seven-day Barman recovery window and fourteen-day R2 hard expiry for current PostgreSQL sources.
  - `pg18-core` and `pg19-experimental` receive separate Barman prefixes with the same policy.
  - FalkorDB emits a nightly RDB to its scoped R2 bucket with fourteen-day expiry.
  - Current-source backup completion blocks only deletion of the current sources.
  - New-target backup completion blocks only cleanup, not consumer cutover.

  `telemetry-01` already exists. There is no new observability stack or standing “observability agent.”

  A short telemetry task:

  - Finishes the existing Kubernetes Alloy/KSM producer enrollment.
  - Adds CNPG port `9187` and FalkorDB exporter port `9121`.
  - Sends those series to the existing `telemetry-01` stores.
  - Adds no new dashboards, alerts, stores, or acceptance framework.
  - Does not block restoration, cutover, or cleanup.

  - `docs/kubernetes/kubernetes.md`: concise routing and CNPG/FalkorDB ownership decision.
  - `docs/observability/observability.md`: updated only after Kubernetes producer enrollment is live.
  - Database names, extensions, schema objects, and representative source/destination row counts match.
  - Forgejo, Soil, the control-plane app, and the historical consumers perform their normal reads and writes.
  - FalkorDB exposes the expected graph keys and still answers after an ordinary pod restart.
  - R2 contains base backup and WAL objects for both new PostgreSQL clusters and a current FalkorDB RDB.
  - Telemetry series appear in the existing `telemetry-01` stores.

## Environment Preferences
- **No Local Containers:** Avoid running Docker, Podman, or any containerized services on this local machine (icarus-laptop). Use remote infrastructure (e.g., raspberryoracle) for these tasks.

## Git Workflow Preferences
- **No Draft PRs:** When opening pull requests, do not open them as draft. Open a pull request only when it is ready for review.
When you stop your work, or are finished with your work, OPEN A PULL REQUEST!
- **Commit Along the Way:** Commit work in meaningful increments whenever a coherent chunk is done. Do not leave all commits until the end.
- **Prefer Existing Branches:** Prefer an existing branch when it already fits the work. Do not create a new branch by default. Only switch to another branch when there is a concrete review reason and an appropriate existing feature or review branch already exists for that work.

# AGENTS.md — required reading and router

This repository is the active successor to `coldaine-k8cluster`. The archived repository is
discovery material, not current technical design. README is not an operating guide.

## Required route

Before investigating, designing, changing, or documenting anything, read in order:

1. [`docs/NORTH_STAR.md`](docs/NORTH_STAR.md) — outcomes and non-negotiables that win conflicts.
2. [`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) — homelab-wide topology, relationships, and
   boundaries.
3. [`docs/CAPABILITY_MAP.md`](docs/CAPABILITY_MAP.md) — capability state and the domain overview to
   read next.

Follow the relevant capability into its domain overview. Let that overview route to focused design,
deployment, procedure, recovery, and active-plan documents. Do not turn this file into a complete
document index or skip the progressive-disclosure chain.

For any documentation creation, deletion, consolidation, restructuring, or placement decision, read
[`docs/DOC_GUIDE.md`](docs/DOC_GUIDE.md) before editing. First determine whether the information is
already recorded. Correct or extend the existing authoritative document rather than creating
another source of truth. If no current document fits, use the guide to decide where it belongs.

## Every change includes a documentation-impact check

After changing code, deployment inputs, tools, configuration, or infrastructure, ask whether the
change alters durable design, current implementation facts, standing procedures, recovery, or
capability state.

- If durable truth changed, update the affected documents in the same pull request.
- If durable truth did not change, say why in the pull request; do not manufacture a Markdown change.
- Use domain documents for durable identity and expected behavior. Query live systems for present
  health, power state, capacity, queue depth, and task progress.

## Working rules

- Authority means the document or live system that records the truth; it does not mean a person,
  team, host, VM, or container.
- Identify every Proxmox guest in human-facing prose by name plus kind and ID, and include the PVE
  authority when placement matters: `pdm-01` (VM 200 on SER10), `haos-01` (VM 111 on SER8),
  `n5-llm-01` (CT 300 on N5).
- Query Doppler directly when an operation requires a credential. Never commit or print secret
  values, and do not create repository inventories of Doppler contents.
- Do not run Docker, Podman, or other local containers on `icarus-laptop`.
- Use an existing fitting branch when one exists. Commit coherent increments and open or update a
  ready-for-review pull request when work stops.
- Use `just setup` to initialize or refresh local cluster context (`~/.kube/config`) before executing Kubernetes operations. Use `just validate` to verify platform manifest rendering after modifying Kubernetes infrastructure files. Design rationale is in [`docs/dev/JustFileTooling.md`](docs/dev/JustFileTooling.md).

+# PostgreSQL Barman/R2 runtime resources are intentionally omitted from this scaffold:
+# R2 credential key names are confirmed in Doppler homelab/dev, but the non-secret authoritative
+# R2 endpoint URL was not present in repository evidence. Rather than commit a fake endpoint into
+# reviewable manifests, primary should add the ObjectStore + ScheduledBackup resources once that
+# endpoint is supplied.
+#
+# FalkorDB's nightly RDB backup shape is fully scaffolded below because it is reviewable without
+# inventing an object-store endpoint.
+---
+apiVersion: v1
+kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
+metadata:
+  name: falkordb-rdb-backups
+  namespace: data-platform
+  labels:
+    coldaine.homelab/purpose: falkordb-rdb-backups
+spec:
+  accessModes:
+    - ReadWriteOnce
+  storageClassName: longhorn
+  resources:
+    requests:
+      storage: 20Gi
+---
+apiVersion: batch/v1
+kind: CronJob
+metadata:
+  name: falkordb-nightly-rdb
+  namespace: data-platform
+  labels:
+    coldaine.homelab/purpose: falkordb-nightly-rdb
+spec:
+  schedule: "0 0 5 * * *"
+  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
+  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
+  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
+  jobTemplate:
+    spec:
+      template:
+        metadata:
+          labels:
+            coldaine.homelab/purpose: falkordb-nightly-rdb
+        spec:
+          restartPolicy: OnFailure
+          containers:
+            - name: dump
+              image: docker.io/apecloud/falkordb:v4.12.5
+              imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
+              env:
+                - name: REDISCLI_AUTH
+                  valueFrom:
+                    secretKeyRef:
+                      name: falkordb-auth
+                      key: password
+              command:
+                - /bin/sh
+                - -ec
+              args:
+                - |
+                  stamp="$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
+                  out="/backup/falkordb-${stamp}.rdb"
+                  redis-cli -h falkordb -p 6379 --rdb "$out"
+                  gzip -f "$out"
+                  find /backup -type f -name 'falkordb-*.rdb.gz' -mtime +14 -delete
+              volumeMounts:
+                - name: backups
+                  mountPath: /backup
+          volumes:
+            - name: backups
+              persistentVolumeClaim:
+                claimName: falkordb-rdb-backups

+# FalkorDB replaces the old KubeBlocks addon with the same pinned server and exporter images
+# evidenced in the repository's rendered addon output:
+#   docker.io/apecloud/falkordb:v4.12.5
+#   docker.io/apecloud/redis_exporter:v1.80.0
+---
+apiVersion: v1
+kind: ConfigMap
+metadata:
+  name: falkordb-config
+  namespace: data-platform
+  labels:
+    coldaine.homelab/purpose: falkordb-config
+data:
+  redis.conf: |
+    bind 0.0.0.0
+    port 6379
+    protected-mode yes
+    dir /data
+    dbfilename dump.rdb
+    appendonly yes
+    appendfilename "appendonly.aof"
+    appenddirname "appendonlydir"
+    appendfsync everysec
+    no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no
+    auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100
+    auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb
+    aof-load-truncated yes
+    save ""
+---
+apiVersion: v1
+kind: Service
+metadata:
+  name: falkordb
+  namespace: data-platform
+  labels:
+    coldaine.homelab/purpose: falkordb
+spec:
+  selector:
+    app.kubernetes.io/name: falkordb
+  ports:
+    - name: redis
+      port: 6379
+      targetPort: redis
+---
+apiVersion: v1
+kind: Service
+metadata:
+  name: falkordb-lan
+  namespace: data-platform
+  labels:
+    coldaine.homelab/purpose: falkordb-lan
+spec:
+  type: LoadBalancer
+  loadBalancerIP: 192.168.30.206
+  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
+  selector:
+    app.kubernetes.io/name: falkordb
+  ports:
+    - name: redis
+      port: 6379

# Shared application Postgres home — first database: forgejo.
# Context7 checked: CloudNativePG Cluster bootstrap.initdb + storage.storageClass;
# operator 1.30.0 defaults to PostgreSQL 18.4 (pinned explicitly below).
#
# Flux declares this with the operator, longhorn-db StorageClass, and
# forgejo-db-owner ExternalSecret; the controllers converge their dependencies.
#
# Barman Cloud owns continuous WAL archiving and object-store base backups.
# The referenced ObjectStore is declared alongside this Cluster.
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: pg-apps
  namespace: cnpg
  labels:
    coldaine.homelab/purpose: application-postgres
    coldaine.homelab/first-database: forgejo
spec:
  # pg18-class — pin matches CNPG 1.30.0 default major.
  imageName: ghcr.io/cloudnative-pg/postgresql:18.4
  instances: 1

  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: 250m
      memory: 512Mi
    limits:
      memory: 2Gi

  storage:
    size: 20Gi
    storageClass: longhorn-db

  bootstrap:
    initdb:
      database: forgejo
      owner: forgejo
      dataChecksums: true
      secret:
        name: forgejo-db-owner

  # Keep Longhorn available for on-demand volume-snapshot backups.
  # className matches ../longhorn/volumesnapshotclass.yaml.
  backup:
    volumeSnapshot:
      className: longhorn
      online: true

  # Decision note (2026-07-21, Codex): Enable Barman at cluster creation so WAL archiving is never retrofitted.
  plugins:
    - name: barman-cloud.cloudnative-pg.io
      isWALArchiver: true
      parameters:
        barmanObjectName: garage-s3-store
# Barman Cloud Plugin ObjectStore for Garage S3 backups (Barman CR API v1).
# Schema verified against the CRD at plugin-barman-cloud v0.13.0:
#   github.com/cloudnative-pg/plugin-barman-cloud .../barmancloud.cnpg.io_objectstores.yaml
# spec.configuration is a REQUIRED wrapper (destinationPath/endpointURL/
# s3Credentials/wal all live under it); destinationPath is required.
#
# Endpoint: Garage S3 API Service is `garage` in namespace `garage`
# (Helm release `garage`, chart service name = fullname = release name),
# so the in-cluster path is garage.garage.svc, NOT garage.cnpg.svc.
apiVersion: barmancloud.cnpg.io/v1
kind: ObjectStore
metadata:
  name: garage-s3-store
  namespace: cnpg
  labels:
    coldaine.homelab/purpose: postgres-backup-store
spec:
  # Decision note (2026-07-21, Codex): Bound Barman base-backup and WAL growth to a 14-day recovery window.
  retentionPolicy: "14d"
  instanceSidecarConfiguration:
    retentionPolicyIntervalSeconds: 1800
  configuration:
    destinationPath: "s3://cnpg-barman-backups/"
    endpointURL: "http://garage.garage.svc:3900"
    s3Credentials:
      accessKeyId:
        name: garage-s3-credentials
        key: ACCESS_KEY_ID
      secretAccessKey:
        name: garage-s3-credentials
        key: SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
      region:
        name: garage-s3-credentials
        key: REGION
    data:
      compression: gzip
    wal:
      compression: gzip
      maxParallel: 2
# ScheduledBackup triggering a Barman Cloud plugin base backup.
# Schema verified against the CNPG v1.30.0 ScheduledBackup CRD: valid spec
# fields are method (enum barmanObjectStore|volumeSnapshot|plugin) +
# pluginConfiguration.name. There is NO spec.plugins on a ScheduledBackup —
# that block (isWALArchiver / barmanObjectName) belongs on the Cluster's
# spec.plugins. The ObjectStore linkage comes from the Cluster's WAL-archiver
# plugin config, so this backup only names the plugin.
#
# Schedule is Go 6-field cron (seconds first): 02:00:00 UTC daily. The
# garage-s3-store ObjectStore enforces a 14-day recovery-window retention
# policy, so backup objects and WAL do not grow without bound.
# Cluster.spec.plugins names this plugin and ObjectStore (see objectstore.yaml
# and cluster.yaml).
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: ScheduledBackup
metadata:
  name: pg-apps-nightly-s3
  namespace: cnpg
spec:
  schedule: "0 0 2 * * *"
  cluster:
    name: pg-apps
  method: plugin
  pluginConfiguration:
    name: barman-cloud.cloudnative-pg.io
  backupOwnerReference: self
  immediate: false
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - externalsecret-forgejo.yaml
  - externalsecret-s3.yaml
  - objectstore.yaml
  - cluster.yaml
  - scheduledbackup-plugin.yaml
